questions.question: What is one benefit of wearing a DOT-approved helmet?

options.text: It limits your side vision.
It can reduce how serious a head injury is.
It is usually uncomfortable.
It makes controlling your motorcycle harder.

questions.correctAnswerText: It can reduce how serious a head injury is.
questions.explanation: Wearing a helmet greatly improves your chances of avoiding serious head or neck injuries in a crash. A DOT-approved helmet will not limit your side vision.

questions.question: What does a plastic, shatter-resistant face shield protect?

options.text: It is not needed if you have a windshield.
Only your eyes.
Your eyes and more of your face.
Your face less well than goggles do.

questions.correctAnswerText: Your eyes and more of your face.
questions.explanation: A plastic, shatter-resistant face shield protects your entire face, including your eyes. Goggles only protect your eyes. A windshield alone is not enough protection.

questions.question: What does this hand signal mean?

options.text: Slow or stop
Left turn
Right turn
Backing up

questions.correctAnswerText: Left turn
questions.explanation: Riders can use hand signals instead of or along with turn signals. When a rider extends their left arm straight out, it means they plan to turn left or change lanes to the left.

questions.question: What type of sign is yellow with black lettering or symbols?

options.text: Warning
Service
Regulatory
Speed limit

questions.correctAnswerText: Warning
questions.explanation: Warning signs are yellow with black lettering or symbols. They alert drivers about upcoming road conditions.

questions.question: How should you help drivers merge into your lane from an entrance ramp?

options.text: Stay in your lane.
Move to the next lane if you can.
Do not worry because they should merge safely.
Ride on the far left shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: Move to the next lane if you can.
questions.explanation: Drivers merging onto the highway may not see your motorcycle. Give them space by moving to a different lane if possible.

questions.question: When riding at night, what speed should you travel?

options.text: Slower than you would during the day.
The same speed as you would during the day.
Faster than you would during the day.
On the shoulder so other vehicles can see you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Slower than you would during the day.
questions.explanation: Ride slower at night than you would during the day in similar conditions. It is harder to see hazards in the dark, so going slower helps you avoid accidents.

questions.question: What is one danger of braking too hard?

options.text: You may lose grip on one or both wheels.
You may stop sooner than expected.
You may pop a tire.
It may take too long to stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may lose grip on one or both wheels.
questions.explanation: Braking too hard can cause you to lose traction on one or both wheels and crash.

questions.question: When riding on a slippery surface, what should you NOT do?

options.text: Reduce your speed.
Avoid sudden moves.
Use both brakes.
Brake quickly.

questions.correctAnswerText: Brake quickly.
questions.explanation: On a slippery surface, reduce your speed, avoid sudden movements, and use both brakes gently if needed.

questions.question: What are the penalties for drinking and riding?

options.text: Severe.
Up to a judge to decide.
Not very harsh.
Optional.

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe.
questions.explanation: Oregon law has strict mandatory penalties for drinking and riding. It is illegal and dangerous to operate a motorcycle while under the influence of alcohol.

questions.question: When do most motorcycle crashes happen?

options.text: On short trips.
On long trips.
After at least an hour of riding.
After more than 8 hours of riding.

questions.correctAnswerText: On short trips.
questions.explanation: Most motorcycle crashes happen on short trips—less than five miles—just a few minutes after the rider starts riding.

questions.question: Riders without helmets are ________ to die in a crash than riders who wear helmets.

options.text: Half as likely
Twice as likely
Three times as likely
Just as likely

questions.correctAnswerText: Three times as likely
questions.explanation: Riders without helmets are three times more likely to die from head injuries in a crash than riders wearing helmets. This is true at any speed.

questions.question: When a group of riders passes another vehicle, they should:

options.text: Pass in a staggered formation.
Pass in a pyramid formation.
Pass one at a time.
Pass in a splintered formation.

questions.correctAnswerText: Pass one at a time.
questions.explanation: On a two-lane road, riders should pass one at a time. The second rider waits until the first rider safely returns to the original lane before passing. Continue this pattern until all riders have passed.

questions.question: Which sign is rectangular in shape?

options.text: School crossing sign
Railroad crossing sign
Stop sign
Speed limit sign

questions.correctAnswerText: Speed limit sign
questions.explanation: Speed limit signs are rectangular with white background and black text. These signs tell drivers the rules for the road. You must follow what these signs say.

questions.question: Passengers should:

options.text: Lean with the operator.
Never touch the operator.
Sit as far back on their seat as possible.
Hold onto their seat.

questions.correctAnswerText: Lean with the operator.
questions.explanation: Tell your passenger to lean with you during turns and curves. They should hold onto your waist, hips, or belt.

questions.question: Taking corners too fast:

options.text: Can cause the rider to go into another lane.
Is better than going too slowly.
Often causes the rider to stay in their lane.
Is acceptable because motorcycles are smaller.

questions.correctAnswerText: Can cause the rider to go into another lane.
questions.explanation: Going too fast around a corner may cause you to cross into another lane or leave the road. Slow down before taking a turn or curve.

questions.question: The best way to handle a tailgater is to:

options.text: Move onto the shoulder to get out of their way.
Speed up to put distance between you and them.
Ignore them.
Change lanes and let them pass.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change lanes and let them pass.
questions.explanation: The best way to handle a tailgater is to get them in front of you. If you can do so safely, change lanes and let them pass. Speeding up may make things more dangerous.

questions.question: When being passed, you should ride in:

options.text: The center portion of the lane.
The left portion of the lane.
The right portion of the lane.
Different portions of the lane as the vehicle passes.

questions.correctAnswerText: The center portion of the lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane when being passed. Riding near the passing vehicle increases crash risk. Riding far from it may cause the driver to move back into your lane too soon.

questions.question: Passing on a motorcycle is similar to passing in a car, except:

options.text: A motorcycle is harder to see than a car.
A motorcycle is easier to see than a car.
You should pass on the shoulder instead of the road.
You must make eye contact with the other driver.

questions.correctAnswerText: A motorcycle is harder to see than a car.
questions.explanation: While passing safely is the same as in a car, visibility matters more on a motorcycle. Motorcycles are smaller and easier to miss. You can disappear into blind spots or be overlooked by other drivers.

questions.question: If one rider in a group wants to ride faster than the others, what should the group do?

options.text: Let the rider go ahead and meet at a set spot later.
Speed up to keep up with that rider.
Split up and let each rider go their own speed.
Let the faster rider lead the group.

questions.correctAnswerText: Let the rider go ahead and meet at a set spot later.
questions.explanation: If a rider wants to go faster than the group, let them go ahead. Plan to meet at a designated location later.

questions.question: When changing lanes, you should:

options.text: Signal, check your mirrors, and turn your head.
Signal and check your mirrors.
Turn your head and change lanes.
Signal and change lanes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Signal, check your mirrors, and turn your head.
questions.explanation: Always signal before changing lanes. Check your mirrors and look over your shoulder to see if it is safe before you move.

questions.question: Which of the following will NOT help lower your chance of a crash?

options.text: Be visible.
Communicate your intentions.
Be prepared to react to hazards.
Hope another driver sees you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Hope another driver sees you.
questions.explanation: To reduce your chance of a crash, you must be visible to other drivers. Tell other drivers what you plan to do by signaling clearly and positioning your vehicle correctly. Keep space between you and other vehicles. Watch ahead for hazards and be ready to react.

questions.question: How can you be seen better at an intersection?

options.text: Try to make eye contact with other drivers.
Always use your headlight.
Wave your arms.
Ride close to vehicles in front of you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Always use your headlight.
questions.explanation: To be seen better at an intersection, always use your headlight. Position your motorcycle so oncoming traffic can see you clearly. Keep space between you and other vehicles so you can move quickly if needed. Do not rely only on eye contact with drivers—they may not notice you.

questions.question: What should you do if your motorcycle starts to wobble?

options.text: Speed up to stop the wobble.
Brake slowly.
Hold the handlebars firmly and slowly close the throttle.
Shift to a lower gear.

questions.correctAnswerText: Hold the handlebars firmly and slowly close the throttle.
questions.explanation: Do not speed up when your motorcycle wobbles—this makes it more unstable. Instead, grip the handlebars firmly without fighting the wobble. Slowly close the throttle to slow down. Move your weight forward and down. Pull off the road as soon as you safely can.

questions.question: A motorcycle that fits you properly should:

options.text: Allow you to touch the ground with your feet while sitting on the seat.
Have a seat at the same height as your waist.
Have a seat 10 inches above your waist.
Have a seat 10 inches below your waist.

questions.correctAnswerText: Allow you to touch the ground with your feet while sitting on the seat.
questions.explanation: A properly-fitted motorcycle lets you touch the ground with your feet while seated. When riding, keep your feet firmly on the footrests.

questions.question: When should motorcycle riders wear hearing protection?

options.text: At all times to prevent hearing damage.
Only on long rides.
Never, because it blocks horns and sirens.
Never, because a helmet is enough protection.

questions.correctAnswerText: At all times to prevent hearing damage.
questions.explanation: Wind and engine noise can cause permanent hearing loss, even with a full-face helmet. Earplugs and other hearing protection stop damage while still letting you hear important sounds like horns and sirens.
